researchStatement: I study how optimization and AI can improve the design, coordination and resilience of operations and supply chain systems.
biography: I am a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus, working with Angela Kitali. My research brings together operations research, mathematical optimization and AI to study scheduling, resource allocation and coordination in operations and supply chains.

Previously, I was a postdoctoral research scholar at Florida State University, where I received my Ph.D. in Civil Engineering in August 2025 under the supervision of Maxim A. Dulebenets. I also hold a Graduate Certificate in Engineering Data Analytics from Florida State University and a B.S. in Harbor, Waterway and Coastal Engineering from Wuhan University.
homeResearch: My research asks how organizations should coordinate decisions when resources, timing and operating requirements are closely connected. A schedule inside a facility depends on what arrives upstream and determines what can leave downstream. I develop mathematical formulations, decomposition methods and adaptive algorithms to represent these relationships and solve the resulting planning problems.

A second concern is how plans should change when demand, capacity or priorities change. I am interested in the value of reserve capacity, inventory and alternative resources, the cost of revising existing commitments, and the way disruptions propagate through connected operations. These questions arise across production, distribution, logistics, healthcare, emergency response and public infrastructure.

My methodological interests include the interaction of mathematical optimization with machine learning and language models: learning which search strategies to use, translating operating rules into models, and using solver feedback to check and improve proposed decisions. Electrification, automation and sustainable resource use provide further settings in which investment and day-to-day operations need to be studied together.
academicContext: My training began in harbor, waterway and coastal engineering at Wuhan University and developed toward operations research during my doctoral studies at Florida State University. The common thread is the planning of systems in which service requirements, shared resources and physical constraints interact.

My Ph.D. research, advised by Maxim A. Dulebenets, examined adaptive and hybrid optimization algorithms for berth scheduling. Related research extended to cross-docking, ship schedule recovery and infrastructure resource allocation. A Graduate Certificate in Engineering Data Analytics complemented this work with training in data analysis, machine learning and deep learning.

After completing my Ph.D. in August 2025, I continued at Florida State University as a postdoctoral research scholar. I joined the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus in June 2026, working with Angela Kitali. My current work combines optimization research with AI-assisted infrastructure inventories and broader questions about operations, public services and sustainable resource use.

I have contributed to projects supported by the U.S. Department of Defense, Florida Department of Transportation and U.S. Department of Transportation. I currently serve as co-principal investigator on research concerning speed-management infrastructure in Washington. My teaching experience includes graduate optimization and freight-facility courses, alongside undergraduate and master’s research mentorship and external thesis committee service.

How can AI assist optimization while keeping decisions mathematically valid and interpretable?
